title: From Privacy to Legal Injury
subtitle: 1890-1950 legal-rights and privacy-injury formation

branches.label: Right articulated
branches.description: Privacy becomes a legal claim rather than only a condition of seclusion.

branches.label: Publicity and press
branches.description: The injury is often exposure: press, publicity, image, name, and reputation.

branches.label: Name / likeness
branches.description: Early statutory and case-law forms treat unauthorized commercial identity use as privacy harm.

branches.label: Tort injury
branches.description: Privacy becomes a civil injury vocabulary: invasion, disclosure, intrusion, appropriation.

branches.label: Constitutional edge
branches.description: Surveillance and home/correspondence concerns begin to pull privacy toward constitutional language.

branches.label: Human-rights language
branches.description: Privacy enters international rights language around family, home, correspondence, and interference.

matrix_nodes.label: The Right to Privacy
matrix_nodes.source_title: Warren and Brandeis, The Right to Privacy
matrix_nodes.description: A law-review article frames privacy as a right against unwanted publicity and intrusion.

matrix_nodes.label: Roberson v. Rochester Folding Box Co.
matrix_nodes.source_title: Roberson v. Rochester Folding Box Co.
matrix_nodes.description: A widely cited New York case rejects a common-law privacy claim after unauthorized use of a person's image.

matrix_nodes.label: New York name and picture statute
matrix_nodes.source_title: New York Civil Rights Law sections 50 and 51
matrix_nodes.description: New York's statutory privacy response protects against unauthorized use of name, portrait, or picture.

matrix_nodes.label: Pavesich recognizes privacy injury
matrix_nodes.source_title: Pavesich v. New England Life Insurance Co.
matrix_nodes.description: A Georgia decision is commonly treated as early recognition of a privacy right against unauthorized commercial image use.

matrix_nodes.label: Olmstead dissent
matrix_nodes.description: Brandeis's dissent links privacy to constitutional limits on surveillance and the right to be let alone.

matrix_nodes.label: Melvin v. Reid
matrix_nodes.description: A California case is often cited in privacy tort history around disclosure, reputation, and renewed public exposure.

matrix_nodes.label: Restatement privacy tort language
matrix_nodes.description: Privacy becomes increasingly legible as tort injury vocabulary in legal summaries and doctrine.

matrix_nodes.label: Sidis and newsworthiness
matrix_nodes.description: A public-interest/newsworthiness case marks tension between privacy claims and publicity or press coverage.

matrix_nodes.label: UDHR Article 12
matrix_nodes.description: International human-rights language protects against arbitrary interference with privacy, family, home, and correspondence.

matrix_nodes.label: ECHR Article 8
matrix_nodes.source_title: European Convention on Human Rights, Article 8
matrix_nodes.description: European rights language protects private and family life, home, and correspondence.
